Two-species competition model with chemotaxis: well-posedness, stability and dynamics

Guanlin Li and Yao Yao
Abstract.

We study a system of PDEs modeling the population dynamics of two competitive species whose spatial movements are governed by both diffusion and mutually repulsive chemotaxis effects. We prove that solutions to this system are globally well-posed, without any smallness assumptions on the chemotactic coefficients. Moreover, in the weak competition regime, we prove that neither species can be driven to extinction as the time goes to infinity, regardless of how strong the chemotaxis coefficients are. Finally, long-time behaviors of the system are studied both analytically in the weakly nonlinear regime, and numerically in the fully nonlinear regime.

1. Introduction

1.1. Background

In this paper, we consider two biological species that compete for resources, with their spatial movements governed by diffusion and mutually repulsive chemotaxis effects. Let us denote by u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) the population densities of the two species, and let the spatial domain be a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary, where n≥1n\geq 1. The time evolution of (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) is governed by the following three effects: competition, diffusion, and chemotactic movements. Before stating the full system of equations, we will discuss each of the three effects and briefly review the relevant literature.

(1) Competition between the two species. The competition effect will be modeled by a Lotka–Volterra-type system [39, 58] for competing species. If uu and vv are spatially homogeneous (thus they are only functions of tt), after a normalization by suitable multiplicative constants, their time evolution is described by the following system of ODEs

{u˙​(t)=b1​u​(1−u−a1​v),v˙​(t)=b2​v​(1−v−a2​u),\begin{cases}\dot{u}(t)=b_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),\\ \dot{v}(t)=b_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u),\end{cases} (1.1)

where a1,a2,b1,b2>0a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}>0. It is well-known (see [35, Section 12] for example) that solutions to (1.1) exhibit different types of asymptotic behavior depending on the coefficients a1a_{1} and a2a_{2}. Namely, in the weak competition regime a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1), there is a unique positive steady state

(u¯,v¯)=(1−a11−a1​a2,1−a21−a1​a2),(\overline{u},\overline{v})=\left(\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}},\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}\right), (1.2)

and it is the global attractor of all solutions with positive initial data. This indicates that the two species co-exist in the long run. In the strong competition regime a1>1a_{1}>1, a2>1a_{2}>1, (1.2) is still the unique positive steady state, however it is unstable, and for a generic positive initial data, the solution either converges to (0,1)(0,1) or (1,0)(1,0) as t→∞t\to\infty, depending on the initial data. Finally, if 0<a1<1<a20<a_{1}<1<a_{2}, there is no positive steady state, and all positive solutions converge to (1,0)(1,0). Likewise, if 0<a2<1<a10<a_{2}<1<a_{1} all positive solutions converge to (0,1)(0,1).

(2) Spatial diffusion effects. If the species have random spatial movements, this effect is typically modeled by diffusion terms d1​Δ​ud_{1}\Delta u and d2​Δ​vd_{2}\Delta v in the evolution for uu and vv, where d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0. When both diffusion and competition effects are taken into account, the time evolution of (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) satisfies the following system of reaction-diffusion equations:

{∂tu=d1​Δ​u+b1​u​(1−u−a1​v) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂tv=d2​Δ​v+b2​v​(1−v−a2​u) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,T),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{1}\Delta u+b_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \partial_{t}v=d_{2}\Delta v+b_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\end{cases} (1.3)

where ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} is the outward normal derivative at ∂Ω\partial\Omega, and the Neumann boundary condition indicates that both densities have zero flux at the boundary. This system has been extensively studied by both mathematicians and ecologists. In the weak competition regime, it is known that the spatially homogeneous positive steady state (1.2) is the global attractor for any positive initial population [15, 19], and there are no non-constant steady states. In the strong competition regime things are more complicated: in addition to the (unstable) steady state (1.2) and the stable constant steady states (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0), the system can have some stable spatially inhomogeneous steady states for some non-convex Ω\Omega (e.g. dumbbell shaped) when the diffusion coefficients d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} are not too large [43, 44]. See [14, 18, 24, 27] for results on co-existence steady states of (1.3) with Dirichlet boundary conditions. When Ω=ℝ\Omega=\mathbb{R} is the whole real line, traveling wave solutions to (1.3) have been well-studied [26, 33, 48, 52, 55]. For further results on this system and related models (e.g. non-homogeneous environment, cross diffusion), see [6, 7, 11, 12, 20, 40, 41, 45, 53] and the references therein.

(3) Chemotactic movements. Besides the above two effects, the two species may also experience chemotaxis effects in response to certain chemicals. For a single species, the most classical model for chemotaxis is the Keller-Segel equation [34]. It describes the collective motion of cells (slime mold or certain bacteria such as E. coli) with density ρ⁡(x,t)\rho(x,t) that are attracted by a chemical substance with density c⁡(x,t)c(x,t). The chemical attractant is emitted by the cells themselves, and it also diffuses in space and decays in time. This leads to the following system of parabolic equations

{ρt=Δρ−χ∇⋅(ρ∇c) in ​Ω×(0,T)ε​ct=Δ​c−c+ρ in ​Ω×(0,T)∂ρ∂ν=∂c∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,T).\begin{cases}\rho_{t}=\Delta\rho-\chi\nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla c)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T)\\ \varepsilon c_{t}=\Delta c-c+\rho&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T)\\ \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T).\end{cases} (1.4)

Since the chemical attractant reaches its equilibrium in a much faster timescale, it is common to assume that cc is quasi-stationary by taking the ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 limit, so that the second equation of (1.4) is replaced by the elliptic equation

c−Δ​c=ρ,c-\Delta c=\rho, (1.5)

and (1.4) becomes a parabolic-elliptic system. Since the primary interest of this work is on two-species chemotaxis models, we will not discuss the vast literature on the Keller-Segel equation. We refer the readers to the surveys [2, 28, 29, 30] and the references therein. Below we will state the two-species system with all three effects, and introduce some relevant literature on similar models.

1.2. Two-species system with competition, diffusion, and chemotaxis

In addition to the diffusion and competition effects in (1.3), we further assume that uu and vv each emits some chemical substance with their concentrations denoted by c⁡[u]c[u] and c⁡[v]c[v] respectively, and each species exhibits chemotactic movements driven by the chemical emitted by the other species. The new system with chemotaxis reads

{∂tu=d1Δu+χ1∇⋅(u∇c[v])+b1u(1−u−a1v) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂tv=d2Δv+χ2∇⋅(v∇c[u])+b2v(1−v−a2u) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,T),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{1}\Delta u+\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla c[v])+b_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \partial_{t}v=d_{2}\Delta v+\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla c[u])+b_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\end{cases} (1.6)

where the sign and magnitude of the chemotactic coefficients χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} indicate the type (attractive or repulsive) and strength of the chemotactic movements. For a population density ρ\rho (here ρ\rho is either uu or vv), following (1.5) (which comes from the ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 limit of the second equation in (1.4)), we assume that the chemical concentration c⁡[ρ]c[\rho] solves the elliptic equation

{c−Δ​c=ρ in ​Ω∂c∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω.\begin{cases}c-\Delta c=\rho&\text{ in }\Omega\\ \frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega.\end{cases} (1.7)

Note that in the system (1.6), the drift velocity for uu and vv are given by −χ1∇c[v]-\chi_{1}\nabla c[v] and −χ2∇c[u]-\chi_{2}\nabla c[u] respectively. Since uu and vv are competing species, throughout this paper we assume that χ1>0\chi_{1}>0 and χ2>0\chi_{2}>0, indicating that both species tend to move away from the chemical emitted by the other species (i.e. uu and vv are mutually repulsive). The goal of this paper is to investigate the influence of the mutually repulsive chemotactic effect on the solutions, in particular, whether it affects the global well-posedness and long time behaviors of solutions.

In the past two decades, two-species chemotaxis models have attracted much interest. Many previous works deal with diffusion and chemotaxis effects only (i.e. the competition terms are absent), where the mass of each species is conserved. In this case, the system often has an associated monotone energy functional (as in the Keller–Segel equation), and many analysis results are based on this variational structure. When multiple species are mutually attracted to each other by reacting to different chemicals, [64] studied global existence of solutions and equilibria using the energy functional. When both species are attracted by the same chemical substance produced by themselves, [25] identified some conditions that lead to global existence and finite time blow-up, and later a sharp condition in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} was established in [13], and blow-up examples for n>2n>2 were constructed in [3]. For a general multi-species chemotaxis model with attraction and repulsion between the species, the steady states of the system and their stability were studied by [31]. For the system (1.6)–(1.7) without the competition terms, various criteria for global well-posedness and blow-up were derived in [56]. When the two-species system has nonlocal interaction, well-posedness of solutions via gradient flow theory and properties of steady states are studied by [22, 23, 42]. See [5, 8, 9, 10, 21, 22] for studies on two-species systems with nonlocal interaction and cross-diffusion.

In the presence of all the three effects (diffusion, chemotaxis, and competition), note that the system does not have any variational structure. When there is only one chemical cc (where cc is generated/consumed by both uu and vv in the sense that ε​ct=Δ​c−c±(u+v)\varepsilon c_{t}=\Delta c-c\pm(u+v)), the parabolic-elliptic system (with ε=0\varepsilon=0) was studied by [47, 54, 57], and the corresponding parabolic-parabolic systems (with ε>0\varepsilon>0) were studied by [1, 4, 37, 46, 60, 62, 63]. In these works, conditions that lead to global well-posedness were established, and parameter regimes for which the constant steady state (1.2) is asymptotically stable were also identified.

More recently, the system (1.6)–(1.7) with two chemicals c⁡[u]c[u] and c⁡[v]c[v] has been studied in the following works. [65] considered the mutually attractive case (i.e. χ1,χ2<0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}<0), and showed that when −χ1,−χ2-\chi_{1},-\chi_{2} are below certain thresholds, the system is globally well-posed and converges towards the steady state (1.2). [17] showed that when |χ1|,|χ2||\chi_{1}|,|\chi_{2}| are below certain thresholds, (1.6)–(1.7) has a global solution, and the solution converges towards (1.2) in the weak competition regime, and converges towards (1,0)(1,0) if 0<a1<1<a20<a_{1}<1<a_{2}. [59] studied the mutually attractive case, and showed that solutions converge towards constant steady states when b1,b2b_{1},b_{2} are sufficiently large. [61] studied the system when c⁡[u]c[u] and c⁡[v]c[v] depends on u,vu,v in a nonlinear way. Let us also point out that for the corresponding parabolic-parabolic system, conditions that leads to global well-posedness and finite-time blow-up were established in [38, 49, 51].

1.3. Our results.

Our goal is to study the well-posedness, stability of steady state, and the dynamics of the system (1.6)–(1.7) in the mutually repulsive case χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0. We aim to explore the following questions:

  1. (a)

    For any χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, is the solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.6)–(1.7) always globally well-posed in time?

  2. (b)

    When χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0 and the system is in the weak competition regime a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1), is it possible that one species becomes extinct as t→∞t\to\infty?

  3. (c)

    What is the long-time behavior of (1.6)–(1.7)?

Our first result is as follows, which gives a positive answer to question (a). It shows that in the mutually repulsive case χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, regardless of how large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} are, the system (1.6)–(1.7) is globally well-posed in all dimensions n≥1n\geq 1, and any solution is globally bounded in time. Recall that global well-posedness has been previously established by [17, 65] under some smallness assumptions of |χ1||\chi_{1}| and |χ2||\chi_{2}|. Also, for any χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, global well-posedness for the system (1.6)–(1.7) without the competition terms was obtained in [56] in dimensions n≤3n\leq 3.

Theorem 1.1.

For n≥1n\geq 1, let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and assume χ1,χ2,a1,a2,b1,b2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}>0. For any non-negative initial data u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\overline{\Omega}), the unique classical solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.6)–(1.7) exists globally in time, where u,v∈C2,1​(Ω×(0,∞))∩C⁡(Ω¯×[0,∞))u,v\in C^{2,1}(\Omega\times(0,\infty))\cap C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)), and u,vu,v are uniformly bounded above for all times.

In addition, for any t0>0t_{0}>0, the equation has the instant regularization effect, in the sense that

supt>t0(‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞)≤g⁡(t0),\sup_{t>t_{0}}\left(\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\right)\leq g(t_{0}), (1.8)

where g⁡(t0)g(t_{0}) only depends on t0,Ω,nt_{0},\Omega,n and the coefficients of (1.6), and in particular does not depend on the initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0}.

The proof of Thorem 1.1 is given in Section 2.1. The proof is based on an energy estimate, where the key observation is that the mutually repulsive nature of the two species allows us to obtain a priori LpL^{p} bounds on u,vu,v that are uniformly bounded in time for any 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty.

Next we move on to question (b) that concerns the weak competition regime a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1). In this regime, for small |χ1|,|χ2||\chi_{1}|,|\chi_{2}|, [17] showed that the constant steady state (1.2) is the global attractor for the system (1.6)–(1.7). Clearly we do not expect this property to hold for large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}: a simple linear stability criterion in Section 3.1 shows that (1.2) is linearly unstable for large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}. Indeed, numerics in Section 4 suggest that solutions can form many patterns for large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}, including some steady states where one species has a much smaller mass than the other (see Figure 3(b)). It is then a natural question whether one of the species could be driven to extinction as t→∞t\to\infty for large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}. Our second result shows that this can never happen in the weak competition regime for any χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, giving a negative answer to question (b).

Theorem 1.2.

For n≥1n\geq 1, let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and assume χ1,χ2,a1,a2,b1,b2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}>0. Assume that a1,a2a_{1},a_{2} are in the weak competition regime, that is, a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1). For any initial data u0​(x),v0​(x)∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)\in C(\overline{\Omega}) that are not identically zero, the solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.6)–(1.7) satisfies

‖u⁡(t)‖L1≥δ​min​{‖u⁡(1)‖L1,1}​ and ​‖v⁡(t)‖1≥δ​min​{‖v⁡(1)‖L1,1} for all ​t≥1,\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}}\geq\delta\min\{\|u(1)\|_{L^{1}},1\}\text{ and }\|v(t)\|_{1}\geq\delta\min\{\|v(1)\|_{L^{1}},1\}\quad\text{ for all }t\geq 1, (1.9)

where δ>0\delta>0 only depends on Ω,n\Omega,n and the coefficients of (1.6), and in particular is independent of u0,v0u_{0},v_{0}.

Note that (1.9) gives a lower bound of the mass of u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t),v(\cdot,t) for all t≥1t\geq 1 (where 0<δ≪10<\delta\ll 1 is a constant that is independent of the initial data), which implies that neither species can be driven to extinction. We point out that it is necessary to let the right hand side of (1.9) dependent on the mass of u⁡(⋅,1),v⁡(⋅,1)u(\cdot,1),v(\cdot,1) (rather than u0u_{0}, v0v_{0}), since an initial data u0u_{0} with mass 1 but very spiky profile (close to a delta function) can have its mass drop to an arbitrarily small number after a very short time, due to the −b1​u2-b_{1}u^{2} reaction term in (1.6).

Our next results concern the question (c). We first consider the case when χ1=χ2\chi_{1}=\chi_{2} (call it χ\chi), and obtain a linear stability criteria for the constant steady state (1.2) in terms of χ\chi in Section 3.1. Namely, there is a constant χ∗\chi^{*}, such that (1.2) is linearly stable when 0<χ<χ∗0<\chi<\chi^{*}, and linearly unstable when χ>χ∗\chi>\chi^{*}. In the weakly nonlinear regime, i.e. when χ=χ∗+ε\chi=\chi^{*}+\varepsilon with 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1, we use a standard perturbative expansion approach to derive the amplitude equation for our system in Section 3.2, and compared the analytical solution to the numerical solution in Section 3.3.

Finally, in Section 4 we turn to the fully nonlinear regime with large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}, and perform extensive numerical simulations that suggest a variety of long-time behaviors in one dimension. Some behaviors are commonly observed in other two-species population dynamics models: for example, when χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} are large, small perturbations to the (linearly unstable) constant steady state (1.2) leads to periodic patterns (see Figure 2 and 3). Also, if Ω=ℝ\Omega=\mathbb{R} is the whole real line, initially segregated initial data lead to traveling wave solutions with one species invading the other (see Figure 4 and 5), similar to those found in [48] for the system (1.6) in the absence of chemotaxis. But the chemotaxis effect also brings us some unexpected patterns: when u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are both compactly supported, for large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}, we noticed that the two densities form clusters and propagates outwards in turn (see Figure 6). In Section 4.4, we also show two examples of 2D numerical simulations in the weakly nonlinear regime and fully nonlinear regime respectively.

1.4. Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we prove Theorem 1.1 that gives the global well-posedness result for any χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0 and any dimension n≥1n\geq 1, as well as Theorem 1.2, which shows neither species could extinct in the weak competition regime. Section 3 is dedicated to the stability of the constant steady state (1.2): we first identify the linear stability criteria, then derive the amplitude equation in the weakly nonlinear regime. In Section 4 we perform numerical simulations in both one dimension and two dimensions, showing a variety of long-time behaviors of the system (1.6)–(1.7). Finally, in Appendix A we briefly describe the semi-implicit finite volume scheme we use in the numerical simulations.

2. Global well-posedness and quantitative estimates

2.1. Global well-posedness of solutions

In this subsection we aim to prove Theorem 1.1, which gives the global well-posedness for the system (1.6)–(1.7) in any dimension n≥1n\geq 1 when the two species are mutually repulsive (that is, χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0). Given a pair of non-negative initial condition u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\overline{\Omega}) with u0,v0≢0u_{0},v_{0}\not\equiv 0, local well-posedness of (1.6)–(1.7) follows from an almost identical argument as [54, Lemma 2.1], which we do not repeat here. Namely, there exists a maximal time Tmax>0T_{\max}>0 and a unique pair of classical solution (u,v)∈C⁡(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω×(0,Tmax))(u,v)\in C(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\Omega\times(0,T_{\max})). Furthermore, u,vu,v are both positive during their existence, and the following blow-up criterion holds: if Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then limsupt↗Tmax(‖u⁡(t)‖L∞+‖v⁡(t)‖L∞)=∞\lim\sup_{t\nearrow T_{\max}}(\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}})=\infty.

Before the proof, we collect some results regarding the solution cc to (1.7).

Lemma 2.1.

Let f∈Lp​(Ω)f\in L^{p}(\Omega) for some 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, and let c⁡[f]c[f] be the solution to (1.7). Then c​[f]∈W2,p​(Ω)c[f]\in W^{2,p}(\Omega) with

‖c⁡[f]‖W2,p​(Ω)≤C​‖f‖Lp,\|c[f]\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\leq C\|f\|_{L^{p}}, (2.1)

where CC only depends on n,pn,p and Ω\Omega. In addition, if f≥0f\geq 0, then

‖c⁡[f]‖L1=‖f‖L1,\|c[f]\|_{L^{1}}=\|f\|_{L^{1}}, (2.2)

and

0≤c⁡[f]≤supΩf0\leq c[f]\leq\sup_{\Omega}f (2.3)

if ff is also bounded above.

Proof.

(2.1) follows from the standard elliptic regularity estimate (e.g. [36, pp. 194]). If f≥0f\geq 0, then (2.3) follows from the maximum principle. Integrating c−Δ​c=fc-\Delta c=f in Ω\Omega and using the Neumann boundary condition and the facts that f,c⁡[f]≥0f,c[f]\geq 0 directly yields (2.2). ∎

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Due to the blow-up criterion that we discussed at the beginning of this section, in order to show that the system (1.6)–(1.7) is globally well-posed, it suffices to show that both densities has a uniform-in-time upper bound. The proof is split into the following 3 steps.

Step 1. Estimates on the mass. We start with a simple observation that the masses of uu and vv are uniformly bounded in time during the existence of a solution. To see this, let Mu​(t):=∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑xM_{u}(t):=\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx be the mass of uu at time tt, and note that Mu​(t)=‖u⁡(t)‖L1M_{u}(t)=\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}} since u≥0u\geq 0 for all times. Taking its time derivative and apply the divergence theorem, we have

dd​t​Mu​(t)=∫Ωb1​u​(1−u−a1​v)​𝑑t≤b1​Mu​(t)−b1​∫Ωu​(x,t)2​𝑑t≤b1​Mu​(1−Mu|Ω|),\frac{d}{dt}M_{u}(t)=\int_{\Omega}b_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v)dt\leq b_{1}M_{u}(t)-b_{1}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)^{2}dt\leq b_{1}M_{u}\left(1-\frac{M_{u}}{|\Omega|}\right), (2.4)

implying that

Mu​(t)≤max⁡{Mu​(0),|Ω|} for all ​t≥0,M_{u}(t)\leq\max\{M_{u}(0),|\Omega|\}\quad\text{ for all }t\geq 0,

2.2. No extinction for weak competition

In this subsection we aim to prove Theorem 1.2, which shows that for two mutually repulsive species, if the coefficients a1,a2a_{1},a_{2} are in the weak competition regime, i.e. a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1), neither of the species would become extinct as t→∞t\to\infty regardless of how large χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} is.

‖u⁡(t)‖L1≥c⁡(α,n,C1)​‖u⁡(t)‖L∞1+nα.\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}}\geq c(\alpha,n,C_{1})\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{1+\frac{n}{\alpha}}.

3. Stability and dynamics in the weak competition regime

In this section, we will derive the criteria under which the constant steady state (1.2) is linearly stable, and obtain the approximate dynamics of the system when (1.2) is “slightly linearly unstable”. Since the system (1.6)–(1.7) has many parameters, to make the analysis easier, let us consider the system where the coefficients for uu and vv are symmetric about each other. Let us set d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1, b1=b2=1b_{1}=b_{2}=1, a1=a2=aa_{1}=a_{2}=a, and χ1=χ2=χ>0\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}=\chi>0. That is, (1.6) now becomes

{∂tu=Δu+χ∇⋅(u∇c[v])+u(1−u−av) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂tv=Δv+χ∇⋅(v∇c[u])+v(1−v−au) in ​Ω×(0,T),∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,T),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u+\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla c[v])+u(1-u-av)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \partial_{t}v=\Delta v+\chi\nabla\cdot(v\nabla c[u])+v(1-v-au)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\end{cases} (3.1)

where c⁡[u]c[u] and c⁡[v]c[v] again solve the elliptic equation (1.7). Throughout this section, we assume a∈(0,1)a\in(0,1) is a fixed parameter in the weakly competition regime.

3.1. Linear stability analysis for a general domain

For the system (3.1)–(1.7), one can easily check that (1.2) is still the unique positive steady state, and since we have set that a1=a2=aa_{1}=a_{2}=a, it can be written as

(u¯v¯)=1a+1​(11),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}\ =\ \frac{1}{a+1}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.2)

whose corresponding chemical concentrations are c⁡[u¯]=c⁡[v¯]=1a+1c[\overline{u}]=c[\overline{v}]=\frac{1}{a+1}. For a fixed a∈(0,1)a\in(0,1), in this section we will perform the standard linear stability analysis to determine the linear stability criteria of (3.1) in terms of χ\chi.

Since Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary, it is well known that the Neumann eigenvalue problem

{Δ​φ+λ​φ=0 in ​Ω∂φ∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω\begin{cases}\Delta\varphi+\lambda\varphi=0&\text{ in }\Omega\\ \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\end{cases} (3.3)

has an infinite sequence of eigenfunctions {φk}k=0∞\{\varphi_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} with corresponding eigenvalues 0=λ0<λ1≤⋯≤λk≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\dots\leq\lambda_{k}\leq\dots, where {φk}k=0∞\{\varphi_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} form an orthonormal basis of L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), and φ0=|Ω|−1/2\varphi_{0}=|\Omega|^{-1/2}. In particular, in the special case n=1n=1 and Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L], we have

φk(x)=2|Ω|−1/2cos(wkx) and λk=wk2 for k∈ℕ+,\varphi_{k}(x)=\sqrt{2}|\Omega|^{-1/2}\cos(w_{k}x)~~\text{ and }~~\lambda_{k}=w_{k}^{2}\quad\text{ for }k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, (3.4)

where wk:=k​πLw_{k}:=\frac{k\pi}{L}.

For a solution (u,v)(u,v) to (3.1)–(1.7), we can use the above Neumann eigenfunction expansion to write it as

u⁡(x,t)=u¯+∑k=0∞ak​(t)​φk​(x),v⁡(x,t)=v¯+∑k=0∞bk​(t)​φk​(x).u(x,t)=\overline{u}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}(t)\varphi_{k}(x),\quad v(x,t)=\overline{v}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b_{k}(t)\varphi_{k}(x).

When (u,v)(u,v) has a small perturbation to the constant steady state (3.2) (i.e. all |ak|,|bk|≪1|a_{k}|,|b_{k}|\ll 1 for k∈Nk\in N), substituting u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) into (3.1)–(1.7), for each mode k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, aka_{k} and bkb_{k} satisfy the ODE

dd​t​(ak​(t)bk​(t))=𝒥k​(ak​(t)bk​(t))+O⁡(‖u−u¯‖2+‖v−v¯‖2),\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}(t)\\ b_{k}(t)\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{J}_{k}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}(t)\\ b_{k}(t)\end{pmatrix}+O(\|u-\overline{u}\|^{2}+\|v-\overline{v}\|^{2}),

where 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} is a 2×22\times 2 matrix given by

𝒥k:=(−λk−u¯−χ​u¯​λk1+λk−a​u¯−χ​v¯​λk1+λk−a​v¯−λk−v¯) for ​k∈ℕ.\mathcal{J}_{k}:=\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda_{k}-\overline{u}&-\chi\overline{u}\frac{\lambda_{k}}{1+\lambda_{k}}-a\overline{u}\\ -\chi\overline{v}\frac{\lambda_{k}}{1+\lambda_{k}}-a\overline{v}&-\lambda_{k}-\overline{v}\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ for }k\in\mathbb{N}. (3.5)

The linear stability of the constant steady state (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}) is determined by the eigenvalues of the matrices 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k}: namely, (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}) is linearly stable if and only if all eigenvalues of 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} have negative real parts for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.

Due to our assumptions χ>0,a>0\chi>0,a>0 and the fact that u¯=v¯>0\overline{u}=\overline{v}>0, each 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} is of the form (ckdkdkck)\begin{pmatrix}c_{k}&d_{k}\\ d_{k}&c_{k}\end{pmatrix} with ck<0c_{k}<0 and dk<0d_{k}<0, thus its eigenvalues are ck±dkc_{k}\pm d_{k}. Clearly we have ck+dk<0c_{k}+d_{k}<0 for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. For ck−dkc_{k}-d_{k}, we have

ck−dk=χ​λk(a+1)​(1+λk)−λk+a−1a+1 for all ​k∈ℕ,c_{k}-d_{k}=\frac{\chi\lambda_{k}}{(a+1)(1+\lambda_{k})}-\lambda_{k}+\frac{a-1}{a+1}\quad\text{ for all }k\in\mathbb{N},

thus c0−d0<0c_{0}-d_{0}<0 (since λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0), and for k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} we have ck−dk<0c_{k}-d_{k}<0 if and only if 0<χ<χk∗0<\chi<\chi_{k}^{*}, where

χk∗:=1+λkλk​(λk​(a+1)+1−a)=2+1−aλk+λk​(1+a) for ​k∈ℕ+.\chi_{k}^{*}:=\frac{1+\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k}}(\lambda_{k}(a+1)+1-a)=2+\frac{1-a}{\lambda_{k}}+\lambda_{k}(1+a)\quad\text{ for }k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. (3.6)

Note that χk∗>0\chi_{k}^{*}>0 for each k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, and χk∗→∞\chi_{k}^{*}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty (since limk→∞λk=∞\lim_{k\to\infty}\lambda_{k}=\infty). This leads to the following criteria for the linear stability of constant steady state:

Proposition 3.1.

For the system (3.1)–(1.7) with χ>0\chi>0, 0<a<10<a<1, the positive constant solution (3.2) is linearly stable if 0<χ<χ∗0<\chi<\chi^{*}, where χ∗:=infk∈ℕ+χk∗,\chi^{*}:=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\chi_{k}^{*}, with χk∗\chi_{k}^{*} given by (3.6).

3.2. Weakly nonlinear analysis for a 1D interval

In this subsection, we focus on the case n=1n=1 and Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L], and consider the regime χ>χ∗\chi>\chi^{*}, where the positive constant steady state (3.2) is linearly unstable. The goal is to perform weakly nonlinear analysis in the regime 0<χ−χ∗≪10<\chi-\chi^{*}\ll 1, and derive the amplitude equations for system (3.1)–(1.7) using a standard perturbation expansion approach, following [16, Section 6].

Let us point out that when Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L], (3.4) gives that λk=wk2=(k​πL)2\lambda_{k}=w_{k}^{2}=(\frac{k\pi}{L})^{2}, thus

χk∗=2+1−awk2+(1+a)​wk2=2+(1−a)​L2k2​π2+(1+a)​k2​π2L2\chi_{k}^{*}=2+\frac{1-a}{w_{k}^{2}}+(1+a)w_{k}^{2}=2+\frac{(1-a)L^{2}}{k^{2}\pi^{2}}+(1+a)\frac{k^{2}\pi^{2}}{L^{2}}

is a convex function in kk (for k∈ℝ+k\in\mathbb{R}^{+}). As a result, in the definition χ∗:=infk∈ℕ+χk∗\chi^{*}:=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\chi_{k}^{*}, the infimum is achieved at either one or two modes.

In the rest of this section, without loss of generality we assume that the infimum is achieved at only one mode (denote it by k∗∈ℕ+k^{*}\in\mathbb{N}^{+}), which is the case for almost every L>0L>0. In this case, we have χ∗=χk∗∗\chi^{*}=\chi_{k^{*}}^{*}, and χ∗<χk∗\chi^{*}<\chi_{k}^{*} for all k∈ℕ+∖{k∗}k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}\setminus\{k^{*}\}. In particular, when χ=χ∗\chi=\chi^{*}, the matrices 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} defined in (3.5) (call them 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*}) are invertible for any k=ℕ∖{k∗}k=\mathbb{N}\setminus\{k^{*}\} and have two negative eigenvalues, and is singular only at k=k∗k=k^{*} with (1,−1)T(1,-1)^{T} in its kernel.

In the weakly nonlinear regime χ=χ∗+ε\chi=\chi^{*}+\varepsilon with 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1, we have χ>χk∗∗\chi>\chi_{k^{*}}^{*}, and χ<χk∗\chi<\chi_{k}^{*} for all k∈ℕ+∖{k∗}k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}\setminus\{k^{*}\}. Therefore, among all matrices 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} defined in (3.5), only 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k^{*}} has a positive eigenvalue, given by

σ⁡(k∗)=ε​u¯​wk∗21+wk∗2,\displaystyle\begin{split}\sigma(k^{*})=\varepsilon\frac{\overline{u}w_{k^{*}}^{2}}{1+w_{k^{*}}^{2}},\end{split} (3.7)

and its corresponding eigenvalue is (1,−1)T(1,-1)^{T}. It means for a small perturbation near the constant steady state (3.2), only the mode cos⁡(wk∗​x)​(1,−1)T\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)(1,-1)^{T} is growing exponentially with growth rate σ⁡(k∗)\sigma(k^{*}) that is of order ε\varepsilon, and all the other modes are decaying. Our goal is to derive the amplitude equation that gives the dynamics for this growing mode.

Since this mode has a tiny growth rate of order ε\varepsilon, we are motivated to define a slow time variable τ:=ε​t\tau:=\varepsilon t that describes the dynamics of the system when χ=χ∗+ε\chi=\chi^{*}+\varepsilon is slightly above the stability threshold. Under the slow time variable, the dynamics in (3.1) can be written as

{ε​∂τu=∂x​xu+(χ∗+ε)​∂x(u​∂xc⁡[v])+u⁡(1−u−a​v) in ​[0,L]×(0,∞),ε​∂τv=∂x​xv+(χ∗+ε)​∂x(v​∂xc⁡[u])+v⁡(1−v−a​u) in ​[0,L]×(0,∞),∂xu=∂xv=0 on ​{0,L}×(0,∞).\begin{cases}\varepsilon\partial_{\tau}u=\partial_{xx}u+(\chi^{*}+\varepsilon)\,\partial_{x}(u\,\partial_{x}c[v])+u(1-u-av)&\text{ in }[0,L]\times(0,\infty),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{\tau}v=\partial_{xx}v+(\chi^{*}+\varepsilon)\,\partial_{x}(v\,\partial_{x}c[u])+v(1-v-au)&\text{ in }[0,L]\times(0,\infty),\\ \partial_{x}u=\partial_{x}v=0&\text{ on }\{0,L\}\times(0,\infty).\end{cases} (3.8)

Next we will express uu and vv as the following expansions in terms of the small parameter 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1:

(u⁡(x,τ)v⁡(x,τ))=(u¯v¯)+∑j=1∞εj2​(u(j)​(x,τ)v(j)​(x,τ)),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u(x,\tau)\\ v(x,\tau)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon^{\frac{j}{2}}\begin{pmatrix}u^{(j)}(x,\tau)\\ v^{(j)}(x,\tau)\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.9)

where we chose the expansion to be powers of ε1/2\varepsilon^{1/2}, since we expect a pitchfork bifurcation. Again, the Neumann boundary condition in (3.1) allows us to expand each (u(j)​(x,T),v(j)​(x,T))T(u^{(j)}(x,T),v^{(j)}(x,T))^{T} in cosine series:

(u(j)​(τ,x)v(j)​(τ,x))=∑k=0∞cos⁡(wk​x)​(ak(j)​(τ)bk(j)​(τ)) for ​j∈ℕ+.\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u^{(j)}(\tau,x)\\ v^{(j)}(\tau,x)\end{pmatrix}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos(w_{k}x)\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}^{(j)}(\tau)\\ b_{k}^{(j)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ for }j\in\mathbb{N}^{+}.\end{split} (3.10)

Once (u,v)(u,v) is written in the expansion (3.9) in terms of ε\varepsilon, their chemicals (c⁡[u],c⁡[v])T(c[u],c[v])^{T} can also be written in an expansion in terms of ε\varepsilon as

(c⁡[u⁡(τ)]c⁡[v⁡(τ)])=(u¯v¯)+∑j=1∞εj2​(c⁡[u(j)]c⁡[v(j)]),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}c[u(\tau)]\\ c[v(\tau)]\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon^{\frac{j}{2}}\begin{pmatrix}c[u^{(j)}]\\ c[v^{(j)}]\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.11)

where for each jj, using (1.7) and (3.10), the term (c⁡[u(j)],c⁡[v(j)])T(c[u^{(j)}],c[v^{(j)}])^{T} is given by

(c​[u(j)​(τ)]c​[v(j)​(τ)])=∑k=0∞11+wk2​cos⁡(wk​x)​(ak(j)​(τ)bk(j)​(τ)) for ​j∈ℕ+.\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}c[u^{(j)}(\tau)]\\ c[v^{(j)}(\tau)]\end{pmatrix}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+w_{k}^{2}}\cos(w_{k}x)\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}^{(j)}(\tau)\\ b_{k}^{(j)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ for }j\in\mathbb{N}^{+}.\end{split} (3.12)

Next we will plug the expansions (3.9) and (3.11) into (3.8), and collect terms of order εj2\varepsilon^{\frac{j}{2}} for each j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} respectively. Note that there are no terms of order one in (3.8), and the lowest order terms are of order ε12\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}.

∙\bullet Order ε12\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}} terms: Collecting all terms of order ε12\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}, we have

(00)=(∂x​xu(1)+χ∗​u¯​∂x​xc⁡[v(1)]−u¯​(u(1)+a​v(1))∂x​xv(1)+χ∗​v¯​∂x​xc⁡[u(1)]−v¯​(v(1)+a​u(1))).\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{xx}u^{(1)}+\chi^{*}\overline{u}\,\partial_{xx}c[v^{(1)}]-\overline{u}(u^{(1)}+av^{(1)})\\ \partial_{xx}v^{(1)}+\chi^{*}\overline{v}\,\partial_{xx}c[u^{(1)}]-\overline{v}(v^{(1)}+au^{(1)})\end{pmatrix}.\end{split} (3.13)

Plugging (3.10) and (3.12) with j=1j=1 into (3.13), the equation becomes

∑k=0∞cos⁡(wk​x)​𝒥k∗​(ak(1)​(τ)bk(1)​(τ))=(00),\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos(w_{k}x)\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}^{(1)}(\tau)\\ b_{k}^{(1)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, (3.14)

where 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*} is the matrix 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} in (3.5) with χ\chi replaced by χ∗\chi^{*}. As we discussed in the beginning of this subsection, 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*} is invertible for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} except at k=k∗k=k^{*}, where 𝒥k∗∗\mathcal{J}_{k^{*}}^{*} has an eigenvalue 0 with corresponding eigenvector (1,−1)T(1,-1)^{T}. Combining this fact with the orthogonality of {cos⁡(wk​x)}k∈ℕ\{\cos(w_{k}x)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, we know that (ak(1)​(τ),bk(1)​(τ))T≡0(a_{k}^{(1)}(\tau),b_{k}^{(1)}(\tau))^{T}\equiv 0 for all k≠k∗k\neq k^{*}, and for k=k∗k=k^{*} we have (ak∗(1)​(τ),bk∗(1)​(τ))T(a_{k^{*}}^{(1)}(\tau),b_{k^{*}}^{(1)}(\tau))^{T} is a multiple of (1,−1)T(1,-1)^{T} for each τ\tau. Thus (u(1),v(1))T(u^{(1)},v^{(1)})^{T} must take the form

(u(1)v(1))=P⁡(τ)​cos⁡(wk∗​x)​(1−1)\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u^{(1)}\\ v^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=P(\tau)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}\end{split} (3.15)

where the amplitude P⁡(τ)P(\tau) can be any function of τ\tau. (Note that this implies that c⁡[u(1)]=P⁡(τ)1+wk∗2​cos⁡(wk∗​x)c[u^{(1)}]=\frac{P(\tau)}{1+w_{k^{*}}^{2}}\cos(w_{k^{*}}x), with c⁡[v(1)]c[v^{(1)}] being its negative.) As we explained above, our goal is to find the amplitude equation, which is the differential equation that P⁡(τ)P(\tau) satisfies. In order to do this, we need to go to higher order terms.

∙\bullet Order ε\varepsilon terms: The equations of order ε\varepsilon satisfy the following, and note that the right hand side contain quadratic products of the order ε1/2\varepsilon^{1/2} terms u(1),v(1)u^{(1)},v^{(1)}:

(00)=(∂x​xu(2)+χ∗​u¯​∂x​xc⁡[v(2)]−u¯​(u(2)+a​v(2))∂x​xv(2)+χ∗​v¯​∂x​xc⁡[u(2)]−v¯​(v(2)+a​u(2)))+(χ∗​∂x(u(1)​∂xc⁡[v(1)])−u(1)​(u(1)+a​v(1))χ∗​∂x(v(1)​∂xc⁡[u(1)])−v(1)​(v(1)+a​u(1))).\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{xx}u^{(2)}+\chi^{*}\overline{u}\partial_{xx}c[v^{(2)}]-\overline{u}(u^{(2)}+av^{(2)})\\ \partial_{xx}v^{(2)}+\chi^{*}\overline{v}\partial_{xx}c[u^{(2)}]-\overline{v}(v^{(2)}+au^{(2)})\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\chi^{*}\partial_{x}(u^{(1)}\partial_{x}c[v^{(1)}])-u^{(1)}(u^{(1)}+av^{(1)})\\ \chi^{*}\partial_{x}(v^{(1)}\partial_{x}c[u^{(1)}])-v^{(1)}(v^{(1)}+au^{(1)})\end{pmatrix}.\end{split} (3.16)

As before, we plug (3.10) and (3.12) (with j=1,2j=1,2) into (3.16). Note that the first term on the right hand side is identical as the right hand side of (3.13), except that all 11’s in the superscript become 22’s. Thus it is equal to the left hand side of (3.14), except that ak(1)a_{k}^{(1)} and bk(1)b_{k}^{(1)} are replaced by ak(2)a_{k}^{(2)} and bk(2)b_{k}^{(2)}. To deal with the second term on the right hand side of (3.16), we first plug in the expressions of u(1)u^{(1)} and v(1)v^{(1)} from (3.15), then use the trigonometric identities cos⁡(wk∗​x)2=12+12​cos⁡(2​wk∗​x)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cos(2w_{k^{*}}x) and sin⁡(wk∗​x)​cos⁡(wk∗​x)=12​sin⁡(2​wk∗​x)\sin(w_{k^{*}}x)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)=\frac{1}{2}\sin(2w_{k^{*}}x) to write the quadratic products into a linear combination of trigonometric functions. After an elementary computation (which is omitted here), (3.16) becomes

(00)=∑k=0∞cos⁡(wk​x)​𝒥k∗​(ak(2)​(τ)bk(2)​(τ))+P​(τ)2​(a−12+c1​cos⁡(2​wk∗​x))​(11),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos(w_{k}x)\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}^{(2)}(\tau)\\ b_{k}^{(2)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}+P(\tau)^{2}\left(\frac{a-1}{2}+c_{1}\cos(2w_{k^{*}}x)\right)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.17)

where

c1=χ∗​wk∗21+wk∗2+a−12=1−a2+(1+a)​wk∗2>0,\displaystyle\begin{split}c_{1}=\chi^{*}\frac{w_{k^{*}}^{2}}{1+w_{k^{*}}^{2}}+\frac{a-1}{2}=\frac{1-a}{2}+(1+a)w_{k^{*}}^{2}>0,\end{split} (3.18)

and the second identity follows from (3.6), which gives χ∗​λk∗1+λk∗=λk∗​(a+1)−(a−1)\chi^{*}\frac{\lambda_{k^{*}}}{1+\lambda_{k^{*}}}=\lambda_{k^{*}}(a+1)-(a-1) (recall that λk∗=wk∗2\lambda_{k^{*}}=w_{k^{*}}^{2}).

Again using orthogonality of {cos⁡(wk​x)}k=0∞\{\cos(w_{k}x)\}_{k=0}^{\infty} and the fact that 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*} is invertible for k≠k∗k\neq k^{*}, we know that the coefficients (ak(2)​(τ),bk(2)​(τ))≡0(a_{k}^{(2)}(\tau),b_{k}^{(2)}(\tau))\equiv 0 for all kk except three modes: k=k∗k=k^{*}, k=0k=0, and k=2​k∗k=2k^{*}. For the k=k∗k=k^{*} term, we have (ak∗(2)​(τ),bk∗(2)​(τ))T=Q⁡(τ)​(1,−1)T(a_{k^{*}}^{(2)}(\tau),b_{k^{*}}^{(2)}(\tau))^{T}=Q(\tau)(1,-1)^{T} for some function Q⁡(τ)Q(\tau), where we do not have any more information about Q⁡(τ)Q(\tau). For the k=0k=0 and k=2​k∗k=2k^{*} terms, note that (3.17) leads to the two equations

𝒥0∗​(a0(2)​(τ)b0(2)​(τ))=−a−12​P​(τ)2​(11) and 𝒥2​k∗∗​(a2​k∗(2)​(τ)b2​k∗(2)​(τ))=−c1​P​(τ)2​(11).\mathcal{J}_{0}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}a_{0}^{(2)}(\tau)\\ b_{0}^{(2)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}=-\frac{a-1}{2}P(\tau)^{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathcal{J}_{2k^{*}}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}a_{2k^{*}}^{(2)}(\tau)\\ b_{2k^{*}}^{(2)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}=-c_{1}P(\tau)^{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}.

Solving the two linear systems of equations using the definitions of 𝒥k∗\mathcal{J}_{k}^{*} in (3.5) with χ=χ∗\chi=\chi^{*} (note that the matrices are easy to invert since they are of the form (cddc)\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ d&c\end{pmatrix}), we obtain that the order ε\varepsilon terms are of the form

(u(2)v(2))=P​(τ)2​(c2​cos⁡(2​wk∗​x)+a−12)​(11)+Q⁡(τ)​cos⁡(wk∗​x)​(1−1)\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u^{(2)}\\ v^{(2)}\end{pmatrix}=P(\tau)^{2}\left(c_{2}\cos(2w_{k^{*}}x)+\frac{a-1}{2}\right)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+Q(\tau)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}\end{split} (3.19)

where

c2=c1χ∗​u¯​w2​k∗21+w2​k∗2+w2​k∗2+1>0.\displaystyle\begin{split}c_{2}=\frac{c_{1}}{\chi^{*}\frac{\overline{u}w_{2k^{*}}^{2}}{1+w_{2k^{*}}^{2}}+w_{2k^{*}}^{2}+1}>0.\end{split} (3.20)

∙\bullet Order ε32\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}} terms: Next we collect terms in higher order ε32\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}. As we will see, at this order dd​τ​P​(τ)\frac{d}{d\tau}P(\tau) finally appears, which allows us to close the equation for P⁡(τ)P(\tau). Similar to the computation of the order ε\varepsilon terms (3.16), for order ε32\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}} terms we have

(∂τu(1)∂τv(1))=(∂x​xu(3)+χ∗​u¯​∂x​xc⁡[v(3)]−u¯​(u(3)+a​v(3))∂x​xv(3)+χ∗​v¯​∂x​xc⁡[u(3)]−v¯​(v(3)+a​u(3)))+(χ∗​∂x(u(1)​∂xc⁡[v(2)])−u(1)​(u(2)+a​v(2))χ∗​∂x(v(1)​∂xc⁡[u(2)])−v(1)​(v(2)+a​u(2)))+(χ∗​∂x(u(2)​∂xc⁡[v(1)])−u(2)​(u(1)+a​v(1))χ∗​∂x(v(2)​∂xc⁡[u(1)])−v(2)​(v(1)+a​u(1)))+(u¯​∂x​xc⁡[v(1)]v¯​∂x​xc⁡[u(1)]),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{\tau}u^{(1)}\\ \partial_{\tau}v^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=&\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{xx}u^{(3)}+\chi^{*}\overline{u}\partial_{xx}c[v^{(3)}]-\overline{u}(u^{(3)}+av^{(3)})\\ \partial_{xx}v^{(3)}+\chi^{*}\overline{v}\partial_{xx}c[u^{(3)}]-\overline{v}(v^{(3)}+au^{(3)})\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\chi^{*}\partial_{x}(u^{(1)}\partial_{x}c[v^{(2)}])-u^{(1)}(u^{(2)}+av^{(2)})\\ \chi^{*}\partial_{x}(v^{(1)}\partial_{x}c[u^{(2)}])-v^{(1)}(v^{(2)}+au^{(2)})\end{pmatrix}\\ &+\begin{pmatrix}\chi^{*}\partial_{x}(u^{(2)}\partial_{x}c[v^{(1)}])-u^{(2)}(u^{(1)}+av^{(1)})\\ \chi^{*}\partial_{x}(v^{(2)}\partial_{x}c[u^{(1)}])-v^{(2)}(v^{(1)}+au^{(1)})\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\bar{u}\,\partial_{xx}c[v^{(1)}]\\ \bar{v}\,\partial_{xx}c[u^{(1)}]\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.21)

where the last term is contributed by the ε\varepsilon term in χ=χ∗+ε\chi=\chi^{*}+\varepsilon.

Next we plug the expressions for the lower order terms (3.15) and (3.19) into above, and again we use the trigonometric identities to rewrite all quadratic products into linear terms. This computation is elementary but somewhat tedious, and we omit it here. Once all terms in (3.21) are written into a linear combination of cosine series, let us only collect the cos⁡(wk∗​x)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x) terms (which is allowed due to the orthogonality of the cosine series), resulting in the equation

P′​(τ)​(1−1)=𝒥k∗∗​(ak∗(3)​(τ)bk∗(3)​(τ))+λ1​P​(τ)3​(1−1)+λ2​P​(τ)​(1−1),\displaystyle\begin{split}P^{\prime}(\tau)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{J}_{k^{*}}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k^{*}}^{(3)}(\tau)\\ b_{k^{*}}^{(3)}(\tau)\end{pmatrix}+\lambda_{1}P(\tau)^{3}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda_{2}P(\tau)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (3.22)

where

λ1:=χ∗((a−1−c2)​wk∗22​(1+wk∗2)−c2​wk∗​w2​k∗2​(1+w2​k∗2))−(c2+a−1);λ2:=u¯​wk∗21+wk∗2>0.\displaystyle\begin{split}\lambda_{1}:=\chi^{*}\left(\frac{(a-1-c_{2})w_{k^{*}}^{2}}{2(1+w_{k^{*}}^{2})}-\frac{c_{2}w_{k^{*}}w_{2k^{*}}}{2(1+w_{2k^{*}}^{2})}\right)-(c_{2}+a-1);\quad\lambda_{2}:=\frac{\overline{u}w_{k^{*}}^{2}}{1+w_{k^{*}}^{2}}>0.\end{split} (3.23)

Multiplying (1,−1)(1,-1) on the left to both sides of (3.22) (and recall that (1,−1)(1,-1) is in the left kernel of 𝒥k∗∗\mathcal{J}_{k^{*}}^{*}, we arrive at a scalar differential equation for P⁡(τ)P(\tau):

dd​τ​P​(τ)=λ1​P​(τ)3+λ2​P​(τ),\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{d}{d\tau}P(\tau)=\lambda_{1}P(\tau)^{3}+\lambda_{2}P(\tau),\end{split} (3.24)

with λ1,λ2\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} are given by (3.23). In order to recover the evolution of the amplitude in the regular time scale tt, we define A⁡(t)=ε12​P​(t)A(t)=\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}P(t), which satisfies the amplitude equation

dd​t​A​(t)=ε​λ2​A​(t)+λ1​A​(t)3.\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}A(t)=\varepsilon\lambda_{2}A(t)+\lambda_{1}A(t)^{3}.\end{split} (3.25)

As expected, this differential equation undergoes a pitchfork bifurcation at ε=0\varepsilon=0, where the type of bifurcation (supercritical v.s. subcritical) is determined by the sign of λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2}. Note that λ2\lambda_{2} is always positive, whereas the sign of λ1\lambda_{1} depends on aa and LL in a rather implicit manner. Using the formula of λ1\lambda_{1} in (3.23), we have numerically checked that λ1<0\lambda_{1}<0 for all a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1] and L∈[0,4]L\in[0,4], indicating that (3.25) undergoes a supercritical bifurcation in ε\varepsilon for these parameters.

Finally, to obtain the dynamical solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1, plugging (3.15) into (3.9) (and using the fact that A⁡(t)=ε12​P​(t)A(t)=\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}P(t)), the dynamical solution near the constant steady state can be approximated as follows:

(u⁡(x,t)v⁡(x,t))=(u¯v¯)+A⁡(t)​cos⁡(wk∗​x)​(1−1)+O⁡(ε),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u(x,t)\\ v(x,t)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}+A(t)\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}+O(\varepsilon),\end{split} (3.26)

where A⁡(t)A(t) solves (3.25).

For ε>0\varepsilon>0, when λ1​<0,λ2>​0\lambda_{1}<0,\lambda_{2}>0, one can easily check that (3.25) has three steady states: an unstable steady state zero, and two other stable steady states ±ε​λ2−λ1\pm\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon\lambda_{2}}{-\lambda_{1}}}. Thus for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1, in addition to the unstable constant steady state (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}) in (3.2), we also expect the system (3.1)–(1.7) to have two stable almost-constant steady states of the form

(usvs)=(u¯v¯)±ε1/2​λ2−λ1​cos⁡(wk∗​x)​(1−1)+O⁡(ε).\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u_{s}\\ v_{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}\pm\varepsilon^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{2}}{-\lambda_{1}}}\cos(w_{k^{*}}x)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}+O(\varepsilon).\end{split} (3.27)

3.3. Numerical verification of the amplitude equation

In this subsection we show the validity of the approximate solution (u,v)(u,v) in (3.28) by comparing it with the numerical solution of the system (3.1)–(1.7). We use an implicit Lax-Friedrichs finite-volume scheme to solve the system (3.1)–(1.7), where we use a fine mesh Δ​x=Δ​t=10−3\ \Delta x=\Delta t=10^{-3} to ensure the numerical simulations have high accuracy. More details of the numerical scheme can be found in Appendix A. For the numerical solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), at each time tt we define its amplitude Aa​m​p​(t)A_{amp}(t) as

Aa​m​p​(t):=‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u¯‖L∞​(Ω),\displaystyle\begin{split}A_{amp}(t):=\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\overline{u}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\end{split} (3.28)

and we will compare it to the analytical amplitude A⁡(t)A(t) which solves (3.25).

In the experiment, we fix the one-dimensional domain as Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L] with L=2L=2, with the competition coefficient a=0.2a=0.2 being in the weak competition regime. By Proposition 3.1, the critical chemotactic coefficient is χ∗≈5.28\chi^{*}\approx 5.28, with the critical wavenumber k∗=1k^{*}=1. We choose the initial data to be small perturbations of the constant steady state (3.2), given by

(u⁡(x,0)v⁡(x,0))=(u¯v¯)+A0​cos​(k∗​πL​x)​(1−1)\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u(x,0)\\ v(x,0)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}+A_{0}\text{cos}\left(\frac{k^{*}\pi}{L}x\right)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}\end{split} (3.29)

with the initial amplitude being A0=10−2A_{0}=10^{-2}. We then set χ=χ∗+ε\chi=\chi^{*}+\varepsilon with various choices of |ε|<1|\varepsilon|<1, so that the system is in the weakly nonlinear regime. Note that for a=0.2a=0.2 and L=2L=2, we have λ1<0\lambda_{1}<0 and λ2>0\lambda_{2}>0, implying supercritical bifurcation behavior of (3.25) in terms of the parameter ε\varepsilon.

For each value of ε\varepsilon, we compare the analytical solution A⁡(t)A(t) to (3.25) (solved by the ODE solver de45 built in MATLAB) t the numerical amplitude Aa​m​p​(t)A_{amp}(t) given by (3.28). The left of Figure 1 shows a comparison between Aa​m​p​(t)A_{amp}(t) and A⁡(t)A(t) for ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 and t∈[0,200]t\in[0,200], which shows that the numerical and analytical amplitude are nearly identical to each other when ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, confirming the validity of our derivation in Section 3.2.

As t→∞t\to\infty, if A⁡(0)>0A(0)>0, since λ2>0\lambda_{2}>0 and λ1<0\lambda_{1}<0, (3.25) gives that A⁡(∞)=0A(\infty)=0 if ε<0\varepsilon<0, and A(∞)=(−ε​λ2λ1)−1/2A(\infty)=(-\frac{\varepsilon\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}})^{-1/2} if ε>0\varepsilon>0. For a variety of ε\varepsilon, we perform numerical simulations of (3.1)–(1.7) and record the numerical amplitude of the steady state Aa​m​p​(∞)A_{amp}(\infty). (In the simulation we actually use Aa​m​p​(T)A_{amp}(T) with T=200T=200, by which the numerical solution has already converged to a steady state). The comparison is shown on the right of Figure 1, where each red circle corresponds to a numerical experiment performed at such ε\varepsilon. It shows that A⁡(∞)A(\infty) and Aa​m​p​(∞)A_{amp}(\infty) have excellent agreement for ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, although the error becomes visible as ε\varepsilon gets closer to 1.

4. Numerical results in the fully nonlinear regime

In this section, we numerically investigate the behavior of solutions of the system (1.6)–(1.7). Most of the study will be focused on the one-dimensional case Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L] with large χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, where the constant steady state (1.2) is linearly unstable, and we are in the fully nonlinear regime. At the end of this section, we also show two numerical simulations of the system in two dimensions in the weakly nonlinear regime and fully nonlinear regime respectively.

4.1. Steady states in the fully nonlinear regime.

We first consider the system (3.1)–(1.7) where the coefficients of the u,vu,v equation are symmetric to each other. We will perform numerical experiments when χ>χ∗\chi>\chi^{*} is in the fully nonlinear regime, i.e. χ−χ∗\chi-\chi^{*} is a large constant. As in Section 3.3, we fix a=0.2a=0.2 to be in the weak competition regime. In order to explore the periodic pattern of the solutions, we consider a larger domain Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L] with L=30L=30. For such LL and aa, Proposition 3.1 yields that the critical chemotactic coefficient is χ∗≈3.97\chi^{*}\approx 3.97, with the critical wavenumber k∗=9k^{*}=9. In our experiment we set χ=20\chi=20, and set the initial data to be small perturbations of the constant steady state. The evolution of the densities uu and vv is shown in Figure 2. The numerical solution suggests that as t→∞t\to\infty, (u,v)(u,v) converges to a steady state with a periodic pattern. The steady state is shown in Figure 3(a), where the two densities exhibit a clustering effect due to the large repulsive chemotactic coefficient χ\chi. Although it appears that uu and vv almost have disjoint support, note that they are both strictly positive in Ω\Omega by Harnack’s inequality for parabolic equations.

Next we consider the original system (1.6)–(1.7) with asymmetric chemotactic coefficients 0<χ1<χ20<\chi_{1}<\chi_{2}. All the other coefficients for the two equations are symmetric, and remain the same as above (i.e. d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1, a1=a2=0.2a_{1}=a_{2}=0.2, b1=b2=1b_{1}=b_{2}=1). When χ2>χ1>0\chi_{2}>\chi_{1}>0, vv is more sensitive than uu, thus heuristically one expects that the cluster for vv should have a thinner width and higher spike. When the initial data is a small perturbation to the constant solution, the steady state is shown in Figure 3(b), which is consistent with our expectations.

4.2. Traveling wave for segregated initial data.

In this part, we consider initial densities (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) that are segregated, i.e., supp​u0=[s2,L]\text{supp}\,u_{0}=[s_{2},L] and supp​v0=[0,s1]\text{supp}\,v_{0}=[0,s_{1}], where 0<s1<s2<L0<s_{1}<s_{2}<L. To see the front propagation clearly, we consider a larger domain Ω=[0,L]\Omega=[0,L] with L=100L=100. The initial densities of uu and vv are chosen to be uniform in their supports and have mass one, i.e.

u0(x)=𝟏[s2,L]​(x)L−s2,v0(x)=𝟏[0,s1]​(x)s1,\displaystyle\begin{split}u_{0}(x)=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{[s_{2},L]}(x)}{L-s_{2}},\quad v_{0}(x)=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{[0,s_{1}]}(x)}{s_{1}},\end{split} (4.1)

where we fix s1=10,s2=90s_{1}=10,s_{2}=90. In this experiment, we focus on the strong competition regime a1=a2=2a_{1}=a_{2}=2, with did_{i} and bib_{i} the same as in last part.

Since the initial support of u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are far apart, for some time the dynamics for both uu and vv are almost identical to the reaction-diffusion equation for a single species ut=ux​x+u⁡(1−u)u_{t}=u_{xx}+u(1-u), where both densities propagate towards the center as traveling waves. As their fronts approach each other, the chemotactic and competition effects start to take place. Numerically, we observe that in the long run, the pair of solutions (u,v)(u,v) converges to a traveling-wave solution (u~​(x−c​t),v~​(x−c​t))(\tilde{u}(x-ct),\tilde{v}(x-ct)) with velocity cc, where c>0c>0 if χ1>χ2\chi_{1}>\chi_{2}, and c<0c<0 if χ1<χ2\chi_{1}<\chi_{2}. Heuristically, this can be understood as the more sensitive species experiences stronger repulsion and keeps receding (thus becomes invaded by the other species), forming a traveling wave. We remark that when the system (1.6)–(1.7) only has one chemical that is emitted by both uu and vv, existence of traveling wave was recently established by [32].

For asymmetric chemotactic coefficients χ1=20,χ2=80\chi_{1}=20,\chi_{2}=80, Figure 4 gives the spatio-temporal evolution for both uu and vv. It shows that once the two densities approach each other (at t≈20t\approx 20), the pair of solutions (u,v)(u,v) forms a traveling wave with negative velocity as expected.

Figure 5 shows the traveling wave profiles for two different choices of chemotactic coefficients. The left figure corresponds to the choice χ1=20\chi_{1}=20 and χ2=80\chi_{2}=80, where the traveling wave propagates towards the left. In the right figure we consider identical chemotactic strengths χ1=χ2=20\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}=20, where the solution converges to a segregated steady state as t→∞t\to\infty.

4.3. Front propagation for compactly-supported initial data.

In this part, we consider initial densities (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) that are compactly supported, i.e., supp​u0=I1\text{supp}\,u_{0}=I_{1} and supp​v0=I2\text{supp}\,v_{0}=I_{2}, where I2⊂I1⊂[0,L]I_{2}\subset I_{1}\subset[0,L]. We fix L=100L=100, and set I1=[45,55]I_{1}=[45,55] and I2=[48,52]I_{2}=[48,52]. The initial densities of uu and vv are chosen to be uniform in their supports, i.e.

u0(x)=𝟏I1​(x)|I1|,v0(x)=𝟏I2​(x)|I2|,\displaystyle\begin{split}u_{0}(x)=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{I_{1}}(x)}{|I_{1}|},\quad v_{0}(x)=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{I_{2}}(x)}{|I_{2}|},\end{split} (4.2)

so that the mass of u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are both one.

For such initial data, our first experiment deals with the system (3.1)–(1.7) where uu and vv have symmetric cofficients, and we fix χ=20\chi=20, a=0.2a=0.2. The numerical simulation is shown in Figure 6, where the first two figures show the spatio-temporal evolution for both uu and vv, and the third figure gives a snapshot of the two densities at time t=10t=10.

Interestingly, as tt increases, both densities propagate outwards, with new clusters of uu and vv forming alternatively over time: once the outmost cluster of uu grows to a certain height, a new small cluster of vv always starts to form outside of it, and vice versa. Heuristically, this phenomenon is due to a combination of the diffusion and strong chemotactic repulsion effects. Note that when a cluster of uu dominates the front, there are still some tiny densities of both uu and vv outside the front, since u,vu,v are both strictly positive at any t>0t>0 due to diffusion. As long as the front is dominated by uu, the tiny population of vv outside of the front experiences a large outward drift velocity caused by the strong chemotactic repulsion, which makes it propagate outwards faster than uu. This additional drift helps vv dominate the space outside of the front, where a cluster of vv starts to form as the small density vv grows exponentially.

In the weak competition regime, when the two species has asymmetric chemotactic coefficients χ1≠χ2\chi_{1}\neq\chi_{2}, we observe a similar propagation pattern as above (the numerical simulations are omitted), except that the clusters of one species are thinner and taller than the other, like in Figure 3(b). Regardless of the pattern, recall that in Theorem 1.2 we proved that for any χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, neither species would become extinct in the weak competition regime.

Next we move on to the strong competition regime, where we set a1=a2=2a_{1}=a_{2}=2 with asymmetric chemotactic coefficients χ1=10,χ2=100\chi_{1}=10,\chi_{2}=100. The numerical simulation is shown in Figure 7, where we find that as t→∞t\to\infty, the more sensitive species vv is wiped out by the species uu.

4.4. Numerical simulations in two dimensions

In this subsection, we perform two numerical simulations in 2D on the system (3.1)–(1.7) where the coefficients of the u,vu,v equation are symmetric to each other. The first example is done in the weakly nonlinear regime with weak competition, and the initial data is chosen to be close to the constant steady state. The second example is done in the fully nonlinear regime with strong competition, and the initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are localized Gaussian distributions. For both examples, our domain is a square Ω=[0,L]2\Omega=[0,L]^{2} with L=30L=30, which is uniformly divided into a mesh of size Δ​x=Δ​y=0.1\Delta x=\Delta y=0.1, and the time step size is Δ​t=0.05\Delta t=0.05. Our numerical scheme is described in Appendix A.

Weakly nonlinear regime in 2D. When Ω=[0,L]2\Omega=[0,L]^{2}, the Neumann eigenvalue problem (3.3) has a family of eigenfunctions {φk,j}k,j∈ℕ\{\varphi_{k,j}\}_{k,j\in\mathbb{N}} where φk,j=cos⁡(k​πL​x)​cos⁡(j​πL​y)\varphi_{k,j}=\cos(\frac{k\pi}{L}x)\cos(\frac{j\pi}{L}y), with corresponding eigenvalue λk,j=(k​πL)2+(j​πL)2\lambda_{k,j}=(\frac{k\pi}{L})^{2}+(\frac{j\pi}{L})^{2}. Using this family of eigenvalues {λk,j}k,j∈ℕ\{\lambda_{k,j}\}_{k,j\in\mathbb{N}}, we can apply Proposition 3.1 to obtain the linear stability criteria of the constant steady state (3.2). Namely, when L=30,a=0.5L=30,a=0.5, Proposition 3.1 shows that the critical chemotactic coefficient is χ∗≈3.7\chi^{*}\approx 3.7, with the critical wavenumber (k∗,j∗)∈ℕ+2(k^{*},j^{*})\in\mathbb{N}_{+}^{2} given by k∗=7k^{*}=7 and j∗=2j^{*}=2.

In our numerical simulation we fix χ=4.7\chi=4.7, which is slightly larger than the critical value χ∗\chi^{*}. Let us take the initial initial densities to be a small perturbation of the constant steady state (3.2), given by

(u⁡(x,y,0)v⁡(x,y,0))=(u¯v¯)+A0​cos⁡(k∗​πL​x)​cos⁡(j∗​πL​y)​(1−1),\displaystyle\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u(x,y,0)\\ v(x,y,0)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{u}\\ \overline{v}\end{pmatrix}+A_{0}\cos\left(\frac{k^{*}\pi}{L}x\right)\cos\left(\frac{j^{*}\pi}{L}y\right)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (4.3)

where A0=0.05A_{0}=0.05 is the amplitude of initial perturbation. In Figure 8 we track the evolution of the numerical amplitude Aa​m​p​(t)A_{amp}(t) defined in (3.28), and also show the spatial patterns of uu and vv at the initial time and after a long time.

Wave propagation in 2D. In this example, we consider the system (3.1)–(1.7) with a=2a=2 (strong competition) and χ=100\chi=100, where the system is in the fully nonlinear regime. Initial densities are given in the form of Gaussian distributions,

u⁡(x,y,0)∼𝒩⁡((L2L2),(σ1200σ12)),v⁡(x,y,0)∼𝒩⁡((L2L2),(σ2200σ22))\displaystyle\begin{split}u(x,y,0)\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{L}{2}\\ \frac{L}{2}\end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1}^{2}&0\\ 0&\sigma_{1}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\right),\quad v(x,y,0)\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{L}{2}\\ \frac{L}{2}\end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{2}^{2}&0\\ 0&\sigma_{2}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\right)\end{split} (4.4)

where σ12=14\sigma_{1}^{2}=\frac{1}{4} and σ22=19\sigma_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}. The numerical simulations of uu and vv are illustrated in Figure 9. We observe that the two densities propagate outwards in ring patterns for a short time, and more complicated patterns start to form once the densities reach the boundary of the domain. Finally, species uu occupies most of the space in the square domain, with species vv suppressed at the center of domain with a high concentration.

Appendix A Numerical scheme

In this section we describe the numerical scheme we use for the numerical simulations in Section 3.3 and Section 4. We will only describe the numerical scheme in two dimensions, since the numerical scheme in one dimension is similar and easier. Our numerical method is a semi-implicit finite volume scheme. The system (3.1)–(1.7) is solved on the square domain Ω=[0,L]2⊂ℝ2\Omega=[0,L]^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and we uniformly divide it into N2N^{2} cells {𝒞j,k}\{\mathcal{C}_{j,k}\} using a Cartesian mesh, where

𝒞j,k:=[xj−12,xj+12]×[yk−12,yk+12] for ​j,k=1,2,…,N.\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{C}_{j,k}:=\big[x_{j-\frac{1}{2}},x_{j+\frac{1}{2}}\big]\times\big[y_{k-\frac{1}{2}},y_{k+\frac{1}{2}}\big]\quad\text{ for }j,k=1,2,...,N.\end{split} (A.1)

Each cell has size |𝒞j,k|=Δ​x​Δ​y|\mathcal{C}_{j,k}|=\Delta x\Delta y and the cell 𝒞j,k\mathcal{C}_{j,k} is centered at (xj,yk)(x_{j},y_{k}), where Δ​x=xj+12−xj−12\Delta x=x_{j+\frac{1}{2}}-x_{j-\frac{1}{2}} and Δ​y=yk+12−yk−12\Delta y=y_{k+\frac{1}{2}}-y_{k-\frac{1}{2}} for all j,k=1,2,…​Nj,k=1,2,...N respectively. We also discretize the time interval [0,T][0,T] as tn=n​Δ​tt^{n}=n\Delta t, where n=0,1,…,TΔ​tn=0,1,...,\frac{T}{\Delta t}.

The computed quantities are the cell averages. For a density ρ⁡(x,y,t)\rho(x,y,t) that is either uu or vv, let us denote by ρ¯j,k​(t)\overline{\rho}_{j,k}(t) the spatial average of ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) over the cell 𝒞j,k\mathcal{C}_{j,k}, i.e.,

ρ¯j,k​(t)=1|𝒞j,k|​∬𝒞j,kρ⁡(x,y,t)​dx​dy.\displaystyle\begin{split}\overline{\rho}_{j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{j,k}|}\iint_{\mathcal{C}_{j,k}}\rho(x,y,t)\ dxdy.\end{split} (A.2)

Note that the chemotaxis term gives the ρ\rho equation a flux η=χρ∇c\eta=\chi\rho\nabla c, where cc is c⁡[v]c[v] if ρ=u\rho=u, and c=c⁡[u]c=c[u] if ρ=v\rho=v. Integrating (3.1) over a spatial-temporal cell 𝒞j,k×[tn,tn+1]\mathcal{C}_{j,k}\times[t^{n},t^{n+1}], we arrive at the fully discrete, fully implicit scheme

ρ¯j,kn+1−ρ¯j,knΔ​t=−(ηj+12,k(x)−ηj−12,k(x)Δ​x+ηj,k+12(y)−ηj,k−12(y)Δ​y)+(ρ¯j−1,kn+1−2​ρ¯j,kn+1+ρ¯j+1,kn+1Δ​x2+ρ¯j,k−1n+1−2​ρ¯j,kn+1+ρ¯j,k+1n+1Δ​y2)+fj,kn+1.\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\overline{\rho}_{j,k}^{n+1}-\overline{\rho}_{j,k}^{n}}{\Delta t}&=-\left(\frac{\eta_{j+\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)}-\eta_{j-\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)}}{\Delta x}+\frac{\eta_{j,k+\frac{1}{2}}^{(y)}-\eta_{j,k-\frac{1}{2}}^{(y)}}{\Delta y}\right)\\ &+\left(\frac{\overline{\rho}_{j-1,k}^{n+1}-2\overline{\rho}_{j,k}^{n+1}+\overline{\rho}_{j+1,k}^{n+1}}{\Delta x^{2}}+\frac{\overline{\rho}_{j,k-1}^{n+1}-2\overline{\rho}_{j,k}^{n+1}+\overline{\rho}_{j,k+1}^{n+1}}{\Delta y^{2}}\right)+f^{n+1}_{j,k}.\end{split} (A.3)

Here ηj±12,k(x)\eta_{j\pm\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)} and ηj,k±12(y)\eta_{j,k\pm\frac{1}{2}}^{(y)} are the numerical fluxes on cell boundaries, and fj,kn+1f^{n+1}_{j,k} are the nonlinear terms due to competition. The numerical fluxes on cell boundaries are computed using the Lax-Friedrichs numerical flux: for example, the numerical flux ηj+12,k(x)\eta_{j+\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)} is estimated as

ηj+12,k(x)​(ρ¯j,kn+1,ρ¯j+1,kn+1)=12​(ϕ⁡(ρ¯j,kn+1)+ϕ⁡(ρ¯j+1,kn+1))−Δ​x2​Δ​t​(ρ¯j+1,kn+1−ρ¯j,kn+1)\displaystyle\begin{split}\eta_{j+\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)}(\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j,k},\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j+1,k})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\phi(\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j,k})+\phi(\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j+1,k})\right)-\frac{\Delta x}{2\Delta t}(\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j+1,k}-\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j,k})\end{split} (A.4)

where

ϕ⁡(ρ¯j,kn+1)=χ​ρ¯j,kn+1​(c¯j+1,kn−c¯j−1,kn2​Δ​x).\displaystyle\begin{split}\phi(\overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j,k})=\chi\ \overline{\rho}^{n+1}_{j,k}\left(\frac{\overline{c}_{j+1,k}^{n}-\overline{c}_{j-1,k}^{n}}{2\Delta x}\right).\end{split} (A.5)

The average chemical density {c¯j,kn}\{\overline{c}_{j,k}^{n}\} on the cells are recovered from either {u¯j,kn}\{\overline{u}_{j,k}^{n}\} or {v¯j,kn}\{\overline{v}_{j,k}^{n}\} by solving the equation (1.7) with a standard central difference scheme, which is implemented with an efficient iterative method.

Since the terms fj,kn+1f^{n+1}_{j,k} in (A.3) is a nonlinear function of u¯j,kn+1\overline{u}^{n+1}_{j,k} and v¯j,kn+1\overline{v}^{n+1}_{j,k}, to avoid solving a nonlinear system of equations at each iteration, we linearize it as

fj,kn+1≈f⁡(u¯j,kn,v¯j,kn)+∂f∂u|(u¯j,kn,v¯j,kn)​(u¯j,kn+1−u¯j,kn)+∂f∂v|(u¯j,kn,v¯j,kn)​(v¯j,kn+1−v¯j,kn)\displaystyle\begin{split}f_{j,k}^{n+1}\approx f(\overline{u}_{j,k}^{n},\overline{v}_{j,k}^{n})+\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\Big|_{(\overline{u}_{j,k}^{n},\overline{v}_{j,k}^{n})}(\overline{u}^{n+1}_{j,k}-\overline{u}^{n}_{j,k})+\frac{\partial f}{\partial v}\Big|_{(\overline{u}_{j,k}^{n},\overline{v}_{j,k}^{n})}(\overline{v}^{n+1}_{j,k}-\overline{v}^{n}_{j,k})\end{split} (A.6)

to lower the computation costs, and note that the linearization does not affect the first order scheme accuracy.

From our discussion above, for j,k=1,…,Nj,k=1,\dots,N and ρ=u,v\rho=u,v, (A.3) becomes a system of linear equations with the unknowns being u¯j,kn+1\overline{u}_{j,k}^{n+1} and v¯j,kn+1\overline{v}_{j,k}^{n+1}. To reduce the computational cost, in practice we implement an incomplete alternating directional implicit (ADI) method, which we describe below. To shorten the notations, let us introduce the following standard spatial difference operators

𝒟x​(ρ¯j,k):=ηj+12,k(x)−ηj−12,k(x)Δ​x;𝒟x​x​(ρ¯j,k):=ρ¯j−1,k−2​ρ¯j,k+ρ¯j+1,kΔ​x2.\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{D}_{x}(\overline{\rho}_{j,k}):=\frac{\eta_{j+\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)}-\eta_{j-\frac{1}{2},k}^{(x)}}{\Delta x}\quad;\quad\mathcal{D}_{xx}(\overline{\rho}_{j,k}):=\ \frac{\overline{\rho}_{j-1,k}-2\overline{\rho}_{j,k}+\overline{\rho}_{j+1,k}}{\Delta x^{2}}.\end{split} (A.7)

We define 𝒟y(.)\mathcal{D}_{y}(.) and 𝒟y​y(.)\mathcal{D}_{yy}(.) in the same way. Thus by moving all unknowns of (A.3) (at time step n+1n+1) to the left-hand side, we can rearrange the terms so that can be suppressed to a compact form in terms of operators we defined above,

ρ¯n+1−((𝒟x​x−𝒟x)+(𝒟y​y−𝒟y)+dd​ρ​f​(ρ¯n))​ρ¯n+1​Δ​t=ρ¯n+f⁡(ρ¯n)​Δ​t−dd​ρ​f​(ρ¯n)​ρ¯n​Δ​t,\displaystyle\begin{split}\overline{\rho}^{n+1}-\left((\mathcal{D}_{xx}-\mathcal{D}_{x})+(\mathcal{D}_{yy}-\mathcal{D}_{y})+\frac{d}{d\rho}f(\overline{\rho}^{n})\right)\overline{\rho}^{n+1}\Delta t=\overline{\rho}^{n}+f(\overline{\rho}^{n})\Delta t-\frac{d}{d\rho}f(\overline{\rho}^{n})\overline{\rho}^{n}\Delta t,\end{split} (A.8)

where the right hand side only contains terms that are known (at the time step nn).

Let us split the operators into different directions, denoted by

𝒜(x):=𝒟x​x−𝒟x,𝒜(y):=𝒟y​y−𝒟y,𝒜′:=dd​ρf(ρ¯n).\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{A}^{(x)}:=\mathcal{D}_{xx}-\mathcal{D}_{x},\ \mathcal{A}^{(y)}:=\mathcal{D}_{yy}-\mathcal{D}_{y},\ \mathcal{A}^{{}^{\prime}}:=\frac{d}{d\rho}f(\overline{\rho}^{n}).\end{split} (A.9)

Let us perform the imperfect factorization of of (A.8):

(ℐ−(𝒜(x)+12𝒜′)Δt)(ℐ−(𝒜(y)+12𝒜′)Δt)ρ¯n+1+O(Δt2)=RHS of (A.8),\displaystyle\begin{split}\left(\mathcal{I}-(\mathcal{A}^{(x)}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{A}^{{}^{\prime}})\Delta t\right)\left(\mathcal{I}-(\mathcal{A}^{(y)}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{A}^{{}^{\prime}})\Delta t\right)\overline{\rho}^{n+1}+O(\Delta t^{2})=\text{RHS of \eqref{Eq: compact scheme}},\end{split} (A.10)

where ℐ\mathcal{I} is the identity operator. Since the numerical scheme (A.3) is a first order scheme, we do not lose any accuracy from the factorization procedure. Omitting the O⁡(Δ​t2)O(\Delta t^{2}) terms in (A.10), we can then write numerical integration process from tnt^{n} to tn+1t^{n+1} in two steps,

(ℐ−(𝒜(x)+12𝒜′)Δt)ρ∗=RHS of (A.8)(ℐ−(𝒜(y)+12𝒜′)Δt)ρ¯n+1=ρ∗\displaystyle\begin{split}\left(\mathcal{I}-(\mathcal{A}^{(x)}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{A}^{{}^{\prime}})\Delta t\right)\rho^{*}&=\text{RHS of \eqref{Eq: compact scheme}}\\ \left(\mathcal{I}-(\mathcal{A}^{(y)}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{A}^{{}^{\prime}})\Delta t\right)\overline{\rho}^{n+1}&=\rho^{*}\end{split} (A.11)

where ρ∗\rho^{*} is an intermediate solution. Finally, we use the Thomas algorithm (tridiagonal matrix algorithm) to solve the linear systems in (A.11).
